units: the writer is writing from a room fitted out under the roof
the roof had been leaking since the cold season
the water that seeped in warped the beams
the warped wood kept the landing door from closing
the tradesman took the door off and trimmed the jamb
two pieces of the roof frame were strengthened
the writer invites the reader to come and sleep in that room
the room has no heating yet
text: I am writing to you from the room up under the roof, the one we called the loft when we were small. Rain had been getting through the covering since the cold months, and the soaked beams swelled until they twisted out of line. That is why the landing door stopped shutting: the wood had shifted, the hinge pulled sideways, the frame went out of square. The carpenter lifted the door off its pins, planed the jamb down, and hung it back. He doubled two rafters as well, since the roof was pushing its weight the wrong way. Now the slope runs clean, the stairwell smells of resin, and rain overhead sounds friendly again. The upstairs room is yours whenever you come. Bring heavy blankets, though, because the warmth does not climb that far yet, and the view over the valley is worth a cold night.

units: an old wall is not plastered the way a recent wall is
the professional compares the old wall to something that breathes
a waterproof coating traps the water coming up from below ground
that trapped water brings salt deposits to the surface
the coating ends up peeling away in pieces
lime laid on in thin passes lets vapor through
a surface that is too smooth must be rubbed back and wetted before coating
this method slows the job down but spares the wall from ruin
text: Should an old wall be plastered the way a recent one is? The builder we put the question to says no, and he sets it out in one image: the old wall breathes, the young one sweats. So what happens if you seal the first of them under a waterproof coat? Damp rising from below stays locked inside, salt works its way out to the face, and the coating blisters and comes away in sheets. What does he offer instead of that? Lime, laid on in thin passes, so that vapor can travel out freely through the masonry. And if the backing is too smooth to grip? Then you rub the face back, wet it down, and brush on a very liquid first pass that bites into it. Work of that kind goes slower, he grants, but the wall stops rotting quietly behind its skin. A face treated so will stand a whole generation with no patching.

units: the manager asks the tradesman how the floor should be fastened
a nail goes in quickly
a nail bends without snapping under shaking
a screw holds better when something pulls on it
a screw breaks if the structure moves
laying a heavy board on joists calls for a fastening that tolerates the wood moving
the screw costs more in tools and in care
the parts meant to come apart will be screwed
text: The site manager asks the joiner whether the upstairs floor ought to be nailed down or screwed down. Nails go in quickly, the joiner says, and they take shaking well, because the shank bends rather than snapping under it. A screw holds a great deal better against pull, he adds, but it shears clean off as soon as the frame shifts under its load. A heavy board bedded on joists wants a fastening that lets the timber keep moving as it dries. The manager weighs up what each way costs him: screws mean a power tool and a careful hand, nails mean a hammer and a steady rhythm. So you nail down whatever swells and shrinks, the joiner sums up, and you screw down whatever you may want to take apart again. On this job, he says, the battens get nailed and the access hatches get screwed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three broad methods came before metal was used everywhere
the first method piles up stones with no mortar
the steadiness of that pile comes from the mass of the blocks
the second method uses clay bricks dried without firing
the third method joins a timber frame to a filling that is then coated
each way of building depended on what lay close at hand
these ways forced thick walls and low buildings
villages built that way are still lived in and kept up the same way
text: Before metal came into common use, the building trade rested on three broad families of method. The first piles up chosen blocks of rock with nothing at all between them, and stands on the sheer weight of its courses. The second shapes raw clay into bricks dried in the open air, bedded in a mud of the very same stuff. The third raises a timber frame, packs it out with a light filling, then has the whole face coated over. Each answered to a resource lying close by: rock breaking the surface, silt from the river beds, the woods along the ridge. Each set its own limits too, in thick walls, low roofs, and steady upkeep. Builders worked around them by turning the openings, deepening the footings, steepening the pitch. Whole hamlets built so are lived in yet, and patched with the old gestures.

units: the stages of a building job follow an order that cannot be changed
a board fence marks out the edges of the plot at the start
the footings are poured into trenches cut in the ground
the walls go up with gaps left for the doors and windows
the roof frame goes on once the masonry has dried
the covering puts the job out of the weather
the pipe runs go through the partitions while they are still open
a coating laid on a damp backing comes away
text: Nothing goes up at random on a plot made ready for a house, because each stage settles what the one after it can do. A board fence marks the edges first, guarding the turned soil and giving the machines a line to work to. Then the footing trenches are cut and filled with reinforced concrete. The walls climb course by course, with gaps kept open where the doors and windows will sit. The roof frame waits until the masonry has cured. The covering then closes the volume and puts the job under shelter. Water and air runs are threaded through the partitions while they still stand open. Coating comes last, then floors, then paint. Swap two of those stages and the bill climbs, since a coat spread on a damp wall lifts away, and a partition closed too soon has to be opened again.

units: a jammed lock set the whole business going
the residents forced the door and made a joke of it
one shove too hard tore the metal piece out of the frame
the bottom hinge gave way under the weight of the door
the dropped door scraped along the tiles
the caretaker wanted to replace the whole thing
a resident who restores furniture won a few days to try mending it
she took the door off and knocked the frame back square
the neighbor came out of it with a name as a woodworker in the building
text: It began with a sticky lock down in the basement of our building. At first we shoved a little, laughed it off, said the door had a temper. Then a neighbor put his shoulder in too hard, the strike plate tore out of the frame, and the bottom hinge ripped loose. The leaf was heavy, so it dropped on a slant and scraped the tile the whole way across. Nothing would budge after that, and nobody dared lean on it. The caretaker wanted the lot replaced and had a quote ready, but the tenant on the ground floor, who mends furniture, asked for a week. She lifted the leaf off, knocked the frame back square with a mallet, hung a fresh hinge, greased the works. The lock snaps shut now. That job gave her a name as a cabinetmaker across the whole building, which she had never gone looking for.

units: an opening that rubs makes a room unpleasant to use
the cause is rarely in the glass
rubbing low down points to wood that has swollen
rubbing high up points to fixings that have worked loose
the shiny patch left by the contact must be sanded
an oil is then wiped on and left overnight
the brackets go back with the holes shifted slightly
a level held on the sill checks that the frame stands plumb
a shim corrects a frame that is still twisted
text: A window that catches spoils the use of a whole room, and the fault lies hardly ever in the glass itself. Start out by watching the gap along the edge. Rubbing low down means the wood has swollen. Rubbing high up means instead that the fixings have worked loose. In the first case, swing the sash wide open, find the shiny band that the contact has left behind, and sand that strip with medium paper until it runs free again. Dust it off, wipe on a light oil, and leave it overnight. In the second case, drive the brackets home once more, moving the holes a shade so the screws bite into sound wood. Then check plumb with a level laid flat on the inner sill. If the frame stays twisted, slide a thin shim behind the upper hinge. Patient adjusting will spare you the price of a replacement.

units: two building jobs are going on facing each other
one of them is a tall block of flats
the balconies of that block arrive ready made
lifting machines set whole face panels in place
that block gains one floor a week
the other job is the repair of an old house
the workers there take the roof off piece by piece
they check the walls and change the timber that has gone bad
the neighbors like the space promised but hold to the mended front
text: Two building jobs face each other along one street, and nothing binds them but the dust. On one side a tower of flats climbs, its balconies turned out of the works already cast, rounded lip and all. Cranes set whole face panels down, and the elevation gains a floor a week. Across the way an old house lies open like a patient on a table. The crews take the roof off tile by tile, sound the masonry, cut out the lengths of frame that have died. Where the first job makes a virtue of speed, the second keeps faith with the joints it uncovers. People on the street watch both and cannot settle it. They admire the room the tower holds out, yet their fondness goes to the scaffolded old front, which will hand them back a street they thought lost. Neither one calls the other useless.

units: the frame that carries the building can be seen from outside
the upright posts were cut with a hand tool
each post carries a horizontal piece that takes the roof frame
the walls are made of three layers one over another
air is left to move within the thickness of the walls
the windows have a sloped sill that sheds water
the ground around the building is covered with draining stones
the roof reaches out beyond the wall and shelters the timber
no surface has been painted
text: Seen from the yard, the shed shows its bones before anything else. The posts, squared off on all four faces with a hand axe, each carry a horizontal beam that takes the trusses above. The walls themselves run in three layers, lapped boarding outside, a vented gap of air, then insulating panel fixed on battens. The openings all share one drawing, a low apron below, a jutting sill cut on the slant to throw water clear, a lintel in one piece. Inside, the floor is a smoothed slab. Outside, a band of draining gravel follows the walls around. The roof falls away both ways and ends in a wide overhang that keeps driving rain well off the timber. Nothing here has ever been painted. The boarding is going silver, the ironwork is taking a patina, and the whole shed ages with no heavy care.

units: building has slowly given up on lasting
soft mortars were replaced by a harder binder
that binder was taken up because it sets quickly
heavy roof frames gave way to lightened structures
those lightened structures cannot be mended and have to be swapped out
thick coatings were replaced by very thin layers
the guarantee on those coatings runs out before the wall wears
each of these choices was aimed at a saving in the short term
the writer calls for materials that can be mended
text: We have stopped building to last, and the drift settled in one careful step at a time. Masons let the soft binders go first, in favor of a stiff cement that sets faster and carries better. Heavy roof frames gave way next to light trusses figured right to the bone, which nobody can mend and everybody must swap out whole. Thick coatings gave way in turn to films so thin that the guarantee on them runs out well before the wall behind them grows tired. Every one of those steps paid for itself on the day it was taken. Their sum leaves us a stock of buildings that will have to come down before they can ever grow old with any grace. A building worth the name will take repair after repair. Asking for materials we can mend is no builder's longing for the past. It is simply plain prudence.
